subproblem.title: Differentiation of a scaled radial cutoff integral with a bounded weight (Simon Ch. 4, 3.4)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (q : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S ε B t : ℝ), 0 < ε → μ (closedBall y S) < ⊤ → AEStronglyMeasurable q μ → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, |q x| ≤ B) → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → Antitone φ → (∀ s : ℝ, s ≤ 1 → φ s = 1) → (∀ s : ℝ, 1 + ε ≤ s → φ s = 0) → 0 < t → (1 + ε) * t < S → Integrable (fun x => φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * q x) μ ∧ Integrable (fun x => ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * q x) μ ∧ HasDerivAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) * q x ∂μ) (-(∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * q x ∂μ) / t) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 3 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 4, 3.4: differentiability of I and J), for a general bounded weight q.

Notation:
- K := B_S(y), the closed ball.
- nu := mu restricted to K. Since nu(whole space) = mu(K) < infinity, nu is a finite measure.
- R* := S/(1 + epsilon). Since 1 + epsilon > 0 and (1 + epsilon) t < S, we have t < R*.
- U := (t/2, R*), an open interval containing t and contained in (0, R*).

1. Facts about phi.
 (a) 0 <= phi <= 1. For every s, s <= max(s, 1 + epsilon), so phi(s) >= phi(max(s, 1 + epsilon)) = 0. Also min(s, 1) <= s, so phi(s) <= phi(min(s, 1)) = 1.
 (b) phi and phi' are continuous, because phi is C^1.
 (c) phi'(s) = 0 for every s > 1 + epsilon, because phi vanishes on the open neighbourhood (1 + epsilon, infinity) of s.
 (d) There is C >= 0 with |u phi'(u)| <= C for all u >= 0. The continuous function u -> u phi'(u) is bounded on the compact interval [0, 1 + epsilon], say by C_0. For u > 1 + epsilon it vanishes by (c). Take C := max(C_0, 0).

2. Derivative in the scale. Let r be real and s != 0. Since d/du (r/u) = -r/u^2, the chain rule shows that u -> phi(r/u) is differentiable at u = s with derivative phi'(r/s)(-r/s^2) = -(r/s) phi'(r/s)/s.

3. Support. Let s be in (0, R*) and x not in K. Then r > S > (1 + epsilon) s, so r/s > 1 + epsilon. Hence phi(r/s) = 0, and phi'(r/s) = 0 by 1(c). So for every s in (0, R*):
 - x -> phi(r/s) q(x) and x -> (r/s) phi'(r/s) q(x) vanish outside K;
 - their mu-integrals equal their nu-integrals.

4. Integrability.
 - Fix any s. The function x -> phi(r/s) q(x) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable (a continuous function of x times q). By 1(a) it is bounded nu-a.e. by B. Since nu is finite, it is nu-integrable.
 - The function x -> (r/t) phi'(r/t) q(x) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable. By 1(d) with u = r/t >= 0 it is bounded nu-a.e. by C B, so it is nu-integrable.
 - By step 3 with s = t, both functions at scale t vanish outside K. A function that is integrable on K and vanishes outside K is mu-integrable.
 This proves the two integrability claims.

5. Differentiation under the integral sign for nu. Put F(s, x) := phi(r/s) q(x) and F'(s, x) := -(r/s) phi'(r/s) q(x)/s. We check the hypotheses of the theorem on differentiating a parametric integral with a locally uniform integrable dominating function (Mathlib: hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le), on the neighbourhood U of t.
 - For every s, F(s, .) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable, and F(t, .) is nu-integrable (step 4).
 - F'(t, .) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable (a continuous function of x times q).
 - Domination. Take any x with |q(x)| <= B; these are nu-almost all x, and for them B >= 0. Let s be in U. Then s > t/2 > 0, so by 1(d), |F'(s, x)| = |(r/s) phi'(r/s)| |q(x)|/s <= C B/s <= 2 C B/t. The constant 2 C B/t is nu-integrable because nu is finite.
 - For every x and every s in U, F(., x) is differentiable at s with derivative F'(s, x) (step 2, times the constant q(x)).
 Hence s -> integral F(s, x) dnu(x) is differentiable at t. By linearity its derivative is integral F'(t, x) dnu(x) = -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dnu.

6. Back to mu.
 - By step 3, integral phi(r/s) q dmu = integral phi(r/s) q dnu for every s in the neighbourhood (0, R*) of t. So the two functions of s coincide near t and have the same derivative at t.
 - Also by step 3, integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dnu = integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu.
 Therefore s -> integral phi(r/s) q dmu is differentiable at t with derivative -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu. QED
proof_key_steps: 0 <= phi <= 1, phi' is continuous, phi' = 0 on (1+epsilon, infinity), and |u phi'(u)| <= C for u >= 0.
For s != 0, d/ds phi(r/s) = -(r/s) phi'(r/s)/s.
For 0 < s < S/(1+epsilon) the integrands vanish outside B_S(y), so mu-integrals equal integrals for the finite measure nu = mu restricted to B_S(y).
Bounds B and C B on the finite measure nu give integrability, which transfers to mu.
On (t/2, S/(1+epsilon)) the s-derivatives are dominated by 2CB/t, so the nu-integral can be differentiated under the integral sign.
The nu- and mu-integrals agree near t, so the derivative at t is -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu.

audit.reason: The one-line proposition exactly includes the prose hypotheses and all three conclusions. The proof establishes cutoff bounds, support, integrability on the finite restricted measure, the uniform derivative bound 2CB/t, and transfer back to μ near t. Signed weights and the zero-measure case require no additional positivity assumption on B. The proof is complete and independent of other children and the parent.

subproblem.title: Integrating factor for the normalized cutoff mass (Simon Ch. 4, (4.3)-(4.4))
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (I L a P Q : ℝ → ℝ) (R M β : ℝ), β < 1 → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → HasDerivAt I (P t) t) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → ContinuousAt L t) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → 0 ≤ I t) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → (n : ℝ) * I t - t * P t + t * Q t = -L t) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → a t = L t / t ^ (n + 1) / (1 + I t / t ^ n)) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → |a t| ≤ M * t ^ (-β)) → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < R → HasDerivAt (fun s => Real.exp (-∫ u in (0)..s, a u) * (1 + I s / s ^ n)) (Real.exp (-∫ u in (0)..t, a u) * (Q t / t ^ n)) t) ∧ (∀ t ρ : ℝ, 0 < t → t ≤ ρ → ρ < R → Real.exp (-∫ u in (0)..ρ, |a u|) ≤ Real.exp (-∫ u in (0)..t, a u) ∧ Real.exp (-∫ u in (0)..t, a u) ≤ Real.exp (∫ u in (0)..ρ, |a u|))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 4-7 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 4, (4.3)-(4.5)), in abstract form. Hypothesis (iv) is the differential identity of parent step 4, and P, Q play the roles of I', J'.

1. Denominator. For 0 < t < R, I(t)/t^n >= 0 by (iii) and t^n > 0. So 1 + I(t)/t^n >= 1 > 0.

2. Continuity of a. Let 0 < t < R. By (v), on the open neighbourhood (0, R) of t, a coincides with s -> (L(s)/s^(n+1))/(1 + I(s)/s^n). This function is continuous at t:
 - L is continuous at t by (ii);
 - I is continuous at t, being differentiable there by (i);
 - s^(n+1) and s^n are continuous and nonzero at t;
 - 1 + I(t)/t^n != 0 by step 1.
 Hence a is continuous at every point of (0, R), so a is continuous on (0, R).

3. Integrability near 0. Let 0 < t < R. For s in (0, t] we have 0 < s < R, so |a(s)| <= M s^(-beta) by (vi). Since -beta > -1, s -> s^(-beta) is integrable on [0, t] (its integral is t^(1-beta)/(1-beta)), hence so is s -> M s^(-beta). By step 2, a is continuous on (0, t], hence measurable there. By domination, a is interval-integrable on [0, t].

4. The integrating factor. Let 0 < t < R.
 - a is interval-integrable on [0, t] (step 3).
 - a is continuous on the open set (0, R), which contains t (step 2), so a is strongly measurable near t and continuous at t.
 By the fundamental theorem of calculus (Mathlib: intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right), s -> int_0^s a is differentiable at t with derivative a(t). By the chain rule, F(s) := exp(-int_0^s a) is differentiable at t with F'(t) = -a(t) F(t).

5. The normalized mass. Let 0 < t < R. By (i), the quotient rule and d/ds s^n = n s^(n-1), the function s -> 1 + I(s)/s^n is differentiable at t with derivative (P(t) t^n - I(t) n t^(n-1))/t^(2n). Since n t^(n-1) = n t^n/t (both sides are 0 when n = 0), this equals (t P(t) - n I(t))/t^(n+1). By (iv), t P(t) - n I(t) = t Q(t) + L(t). So the derivative equals Q(t)/t^n + L(t)/t^(n+1).

6. By (v) and step 1, a(t)(1 + I(t)/t^n) = L(t)/t^(n+1).

7. Proof of (A). Let 0 < t < R. By the product rule and steps 4-6,
 Psi'(t) = F'(t)(1 + I(t)/t^n) + F(t)(Q(t)/t^n + L(t)/t^(n+1))
 = -a(t) F(t)(1 + I(t)/t^n) + F(t) Q(t)/t^n + F(t) a(t)(1 + I(t)/t^n)
 = F(t) Q(t)/t^n = exp(-int_0^t a) Q(t)/t^n.

8. Proof of (B). Let 0 < t <= rho < R. By step 3 applied to rho, a is interval-integrable on [0, rho]; hence so is |a|. Then |int_0^t a| <= int_0^t |a| <= int_0^rho |a|. The second inequality holds because |a| >= 0 and [0, t] is contained in [0, rho]. Therefore -int_0^rho |a| <= -int_0^t a <= int_0^rho |a|, and (B) follows because exp is increasing. QED
proof_key_steps: 1 + I/t^n >= 1, so a = (L/t^(n+1))/(1 + I/t^n) is continuous on (0,R).
|a| <= M t^(-beta) with beta < 1 makes a interval-integrable on [0,t] for every t in (0,R).
By the FTC and the chain rule, F = exp(-int_0^t a) satisfies F' = -aF on (0,R).
(1 + I/t^n)' = (tP - nI)/t^(n+1) = Q/t^n + L/t^(n+1) = Q/t^n + a(1 + I/t^n), using (iv) and (v).
By the product rule, Psi' = F Q/t^n.
|int_0^t a| <= int_0^t |a| <= int_0^rho |a| gives exp(-int_0^rho|a|) <= F(t) <= exp(int_0^rho|a|).

audit.reason: The exact type matches both conclusions and all six hypotheses, with natural powers in denominators and real power in the growth bound. The proof correctly establishes denominator positivity, continuity of a, integrability near zero using β<1, the FTC derivative, product-rule cancellation, and exponential bounds. The endpoint zero is Lebesgue-null, and n=0 is explicitly handled. No sibling or parent result is assumed.

subproblem.title: Continuity in the scale of the cutoff curvature pairing (Simon Ch. 4, 4.1-4.3)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (H : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S ε t : ℝ), 0 < ε → IntegrableOn H (closedBall y S) μ → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → Antitone φ → (∀ s : ℝ, s ≤ 1 → φ s = 1) → (∀ s : ℝ, 1 + ε ≤ s → φ s = 0) → 0 < t → (1 + ε) * t < S → ContinuousAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) * inner ℝ (x - y) (H x) ∂μ) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: last sentence of step 3 of the parent proof (continuity of L by dominated convergence with the bound S |H| 1_{B_S(y)}).

Notation:
- K := B_S(y), the closed ball.
- nu := mu restricted to K. By hypothesis H is nu-integrable.
- R* := S/(1 + epsilon). Then t < R*, because 1 + epsilon > 0 and (1 + epsilon) t < S.

1. Facts about phi. 0 <= phi <= 1, because phi(s) >= phi(max(s, 1 + epsilon)) = 0 and phi(s) <= phi(min(s, 1)) = 1 (phi nonincreasing). phi is continuous, being C^1.

2. Support. Let s be in (0, R*) and x not in K. Then r = |x - y| > S > (1 + epsilon) s, so r/s >= 1 + epsilon and phi(r/s) = 0. Hence for every s in (0, R*) the integrand of L(s) vanishes outside K, and L(s) = integral phi(r/s)(x - y).H dnu.

3. Dominated continuity for the nu-integral at t. We check the hypotheses of the continuity theorem for parametric integrals (dominated convergence; Mathlib: continuousAt_of_dominated).
 - Measurability. For every s, x -> phi(r/s) is continuous. The map x -> (x - y).H(x) is the inner product of the continuous map x -> x - y and the nu-a.e. strongly measurable H, so it is nu-a.e. strongly measurable. Hence their product is nu-a.e. strongly measurable.
 - Domination. Let s be arbitrary and x in K (nu-almost every x is in K), so |x - y| <= S. By step 1 and Cauchy-Schwarz, |phi(r/s)(x - y).H(x)| <= 1 * |x - y| |H(x)| <= S |H(x)|.
 - The dominating function S |H| is nu-integrable.
 - Pointwise continuity. For every x, s -> phi(r/s)(x - y).H(x) is continuous at t, because t != 0 and phi is continuous.
 Hence s -> integral phi(r/s)(x - y).H dnu is continuous at t.

4. By step 2, this function coincides with L on the neighbourhood (0, R*) of t. So L is continuous at t. QED
proof_key_steps: 0 <= phi <= 1 and phi is continuous.
For 0 < s < S/(1+epsilon) the integrand vanishes outside B_S(y), so L(s) equals the integral against nu = mu restricted to B_S(y).
The integrands are measurable, dominated by S|H| (Cauchy-Schwarz with |x-y| <= S on the ball) and continuous in s, so dominated convergence gives continuity at t.
The nu-integral agrees with L near t, so L is continuous at t.

audit.reason: The type matches the complete prose statement. Restricted measurability, domination by the integrable function S‖H‖, and pointwise continuity justify dominated continuity; local support equality transfers it to the stated integral. No finiteness assumption on μ(closedBall y S) is needed or silently introduced. The proof is complete and non-circular.

subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (w : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (φ Ψ F : ℝ → ℝ) (S ε c σ ρ : ℝ), 0 < ε → μ (closedBall y S) < ⊤ → AEStronglyMeasurable w μ → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, 0 ≤ w x ∧ w x ≤ 1) → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → Antitone φ → (∀ s : ℝ, s ≤ 1 → φ s = 1) → (∀ s : ℝ, 1 + ε ≤ s → φ s = 0) → 0 < σ → σ ≤ ρ → (1 + ε) * ρ < S → (∀ t : ℝ, σ ≤ t → t ≤ ρ → Real.exp (-c) ≤ F t ∧ F t ≤ Real.exp c) → (∀ t : ℝ, σ ≤ t → t ≤ ρ → HasDerivAt Ψ (F t * ((-(∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * w x ∂μ) / t) / t ^ n)) t) → Real.exp (-c) * ∫ x, (φ (‖x - y‖ / ρ) - φ (‖x - y‖ / σ)) * (w x / ‖x - y‖ ^ n) ∂μ ≤ Ψ ρ - Ψ σ ∧ Ψ ρ - Ψ σ ≤ Real.exp c * (1 + ε) ^ n * ∫ x, (φ (‖x - y‖ / ρ) - φ (‖x - y‖ / σ)) * (w x / ‖x - y‖ ^ n) ∂μ
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 7-10 of the parent proof, i.e. Simon Ch. 4, 3.4 -> 3.5 ('by integration in 3.4') with the corrected prefactors. We use the pointwise inequality of parent step 9,
 r^(-n) d_t phi(r/t) <= t^(-n) d_t phi(r/t) <= (1 + epsilon)^n r^(-n) d_t phi(r/t),
but integrate it first in x at fixed t and then in t. Integrating in this order compares derivatives directly and needs no exchange of integrals (Fubini). The sibling theorem cutoff_derivative is: for an a.e.-bounded, a.e. strongly measurable weight q with |q| <= B a.e., 0 < t and (1 + epsilon) t < S, the functions phi(r/t) q and (r/t) phi'(r/t) q are mu-integrable and s -> integral phi(r/s) q dmu has derivative -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu at t.

0. Admissible radii. For t in [sigma, rho], t >= sigma > 0 and (1 + epsilon) t <= (1 + epsilon) rho < S. So cutoff_derivative applies at every t in [sigma, rho].

1. Facts about phi.
 - phi'(s) = 0 for s < 1, because phi = 1 on the open neighbourhood (-infinity, 1) of s.
 - phi'(s) = 0 for s > 1 + epsilon, because phi = 0 on (1 + epsilon, infinity).
 - phi' <= 0 everywhere, because phi is nonincreasing and differentiable.

2. Comparison weight. Put q(x) := w(x)/max(sigma, r)^n.
 - q is mu-a.e. strongly measurable: w is a.e. strongly measurable, and x -> max(sigma, r)^n is continuous and positive since max(sigma, r) >= sigma > 0.
 - For mu-a.e. x we have 0 <= w(x) <= 1, so |q(x)| <= 1/max(sigma, r)^n <= 1/sigma^n.
 - Also |w| <= 1 mu-a.e.

3. Sibling facts. Let G(s) := integral phi(r/s) q dmu for real s. For t in [sigma, rho] put G'(t) := -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu.
 - cutoff_derivative with weight q and bound B = sigma^(-n), at every t in [sigma, rho]: x -> phi(r/t) q(x) and x -> (r/t) phi'(r/t) q(x) are mu-integrable, and G is differentiable at t with derivative G'(t).
 - cutoff_derivative with weight w and bound B = 1: x -> (r/t) phi'(r/t) w(x) is mu-integrable.

4. Pointwise squeeze. Fix t in [sigma, rho] and put D(x) := -(r/t) phi'(r/t)/t, the t-derivative of phi(r/t). Then D >= 0, since r/t >= 0, phi' <= 0 and t > 0. Claim: for mu-a.e. x (those with 0 <= w(x) <= 1),
 D q <= D w/t^n <= (1 + epsilon)^n D q, and D q >= 0.
 - If phi'(r/t) = 0, then D(x) = 0 and all quantities vanish.
 - Otherwise step 1 forces 1 <= r/t <= 1 + epsilon, i.e. t <= r <= (1 + epsilon) t. In particular r >= t >= sigma > 0, so max(sigma, r) = r and q(x) = w(x)/r^n. Moreover D w >= 0 and t^n <= r^n <= (1 + epsilon)^n t^n. Hence D w/r^n <= D w/t^n, D w/t^n <= (1 + epsilon)^n D w/r^n, and D w/r^n >= 0.

5. Integrated squeeze.
 - By linearity, G'(t) = integral D q dmu and J'(t)/t^n = integral D w/t^n dmu.
 - Both integrands are mu-integrable: they are constant multiples of the integrable functions of step 3.
 Integrating step 4 (monotonicity of the integral) gives, for every t in [sigma, rho],
 G'(t) <= J'(t)/t^n <= (1 + epsilon)^n G'(t) and G'(t) >= 0.

6. Derivative comparison. Let t be in [sigma, rho]. By step 5, J'(t)/t^n >= G'(t) >= 0. Together with e^(-c) <= F(t) <= e^c:
 Psi'(t) = F(t) J'(t)/t^n >= e^(-c) J'(t)/t^n >= e^(-c) G'(t),
 Psi'(t) = F(t) J'(t)/t^n <= e^c J'(t)/t^n <= e^c (1 + epsilon)^n G'(t).

7. Integration over [sigma, rho]. Let f_1 := Psi - e^(-c) G and f_2 := e^c (1 + epsilon)^n G - Psi.
 - Both are differentiable at every point of [sigma, rho] (step 3 and the hypothesis on Psi), with nonnegative derivatives there (step 6).
 - A function differentiable at every point of [sigma, rho] is continuous on [sigma, rho]. If its derivative is >= 0 on (sigma, rho), the mean value theorem shows it is nondecreasing on [sigma, rho].
 Thus f_i(sigma) <= f_i(rho) for i = 1, 2, i.e.
 e^(-c)(G(rho) - G(sigma)) <= Psi(rho) - Psi(sigma) <= e^c (1 + epsilon)^n (G(rho) - G(sigma)).

8. Identification of A. By step 3 at t = rho and t = sigma, phi(r/rho) q and phi(r/sigma) q are mu-integrable. So G(rho) - G(sigma) = integral (phi(r/rho) - phi(r/sigma)) q dmu. For every x, (phi(r/rho) - phi(r/sigma)) q(x) = (phi(r/rho) - phi(r/sigma)) w(x)/r^n:
 - if r <= sigma, then r/sigma <= 1 and r/rho <= 1 (as r <= sigma <= rho). So phi(r/rho) = phi(r/sigma) = 1 and both sides vanish; this case includes x = y;
 - if r > sigma, then max(sigma, r) = r and q(x) = w(x)/r^n.
 Hence G(rho) - G(sigma) = A, and step 7 is the assertion. QED
proof_key_steps: Every t in [sigma, rho] is admissible for cutoff_derivative; phi' = 0 outside [1, 1+epsilon], and phi' <= 0.
With the comparison weight q = w/max(sigma, r)^n, |q| <= sigma^(-n), G(t) = integral phi(r/t) q dmu has derivative G'(t) = -(1/t) integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) q dmu.
Where d_t phi(r/t) != 0 we have t <= r <= (1+epsilon)t and q = w/r^n, so D q <= D w/t^n <= (1+epsilon)^n D q. Integrating in x gives G' <= J'/t^n <= (1+epsilon)^n G' and G' >= 0.
With e^(-c) <= F <= e^c, e^(-c) G' <= Psi' <= e^c (1+epsilon)^n G' on [sigma, rho].
By the mean value theorem, e^(-c)(G(rho)-G(sigma)) <= Psi(rho)-Psi(sigma) <= e^c (1+epsilon)^n (G(rho)-G(sigma)).
G(rho) - G(sigma) = A, because phi(r/rho) - phi(r/sigma) = 0 for r <= sigma and q = w/r^n for r > sigma.

audit.reason: The type exactly matches the hypotheses and squeeze. The proof verifies the bounded comparison weight, validly applies cutoff_derivative at every admissible radius, integrates the pointwise derivative comparison, and uses the mean value theorem with justified endpoint continuity. Identification of the comparison-mass increment with A handles r=0 and σ=ρ. Its only dependency is correctly declared and acyclic; neither Fubini nor unassumed continuity of F is required.
